newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia export earnings growth seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia export earnings growth seen slowing.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) on Tuesday forecast Australian commodities export earnings growth of 2.5 percent in 1996/97, with minerals and energy the strongest sectors.
In its December quarter outlook, ABARE forecast that the 1996/97 value of Australian commodity exports would rise 2.5 percent to a total value of A$58.92 billion.
That compares with a forecast three months ago of A$59.72 billion and a June quarter forecast of A$61.08 billion.
ABARE said the value of minerals and energy were seen up 4.5 percent in 1996/97, reaching a new high of A$36.3 billion.
Strong crude oil earnings, rising A$425 million on higher prices and volumes, were a major factor.
Earnings from iron ore and LNG were also forecast to show strong rises.
Export earnings from agricultural commodities were forecast to be A$22.6 billion, slightly down from last year's level.
Despite an expected bumper wheat crop, the value of wheat exports was expected to fall by around nine percent as world prices fell.
Export earnings for beef and sugar were also seen falling in the current fiscal year.
ABARE, the Australian government's main commodity forecasting agency, said the world indicator price for wheat was expected to fall after rising strongly last year.
Pool returns to Australian growers was expected to fall 29 percent to A$185 a tonne.
For beef, Australian saleyard prices were expected to fall by 12 percent to an average of 155c/kg in 1996/97 as U.S. meat supplies remain high and competition in export markets remains strong.
The average eastern market indicator for wool was forecast to ease to 600 cents a kg in 1996/97.
The volume of farm production was forecast to rise by 7.4 percent in 1996/97 after a 15 percent rise in 1995/96 in the aftermath of the previous year's drought.
The volume of mine production was seen up by 5.4 percent, similar to the increase last fiscal year.
Wool exports were seen rising in 1996/97, with Chinese demand remaining firm, although production was expected to decline marginally and prices were expected to fall.

ABARE said calendar year 1996 had been mixed for resource prices -- average world prices for most metals declined, some significantly, while prices rose for most energy commodities, particularly metallurgical coal, oil and uranium.
But it said signs of increasing economic growth in most regions of the world and expectation of further increases in 1997, meant world demand for minerals, metals and energy was forecast to rise.

"Stronger metal demands in 1997, especially in Asia, Western Europe, Russia and North America, is expected to lead to falling stocks and firmer prices. The exception is expected to be copper, with substantial growth in world supply forecast to contribute to a rise in stocks and some easing in prices," it added.

Despite that firmer outlook, however, average prices received by Australia's minerals and energy exporters were forecast to fall by 2.4 percent in 1996/97, in part because of an assumed appreciation of the Australian dollar.

"While average prices received for Australian minerals and metals exports are forecast to decline by 5.4 percent in 1996/97, average prices received for energy exports are forecast to increase by 2.4 percent," ABARE said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
